Iran International, published 22 Nov 2026 (curl; key passage: JMIC report, tracking data)

The center reported continued Revolutionary Guards activity involving drone overflights, surveillance of commercial ships and occasional radio warnings. It said Iranian claims that tankers had struck naval mines remained unconfirmed by official authorities.Commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remained severely restricted. According to the report, tracking data showed no recorded transits by cargo-carrying vessels above 1,000 deadweight tons between November 19 and 21.

"])•••$RC("B:4","S:4")More Stories'Happy Ending' pushes the limits of Iran's underground cinemaNov 22, 2026, 16:37 GMT+0•Mo AbdiListen to this article100%A scene from Atena Mahmoudi's Happy Ending, an underground Iranian film that premiered at the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival in Estonia without its makers, who are banned from leaving Iran.Happy Ending, Atena Mahmoudi's underground first feature about a young Tehran masseuse trying to leave Iran, premiered at Estonia's Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival without its makers, who are banned from leaving the country.

The film, shown in the first feature competition of the festival's 30th edition, was made without a state permit. Security agents raided the production and seized footage, but the filmmakers managed to save a copy and finish it. It reached Tallinn as one of a growing number of Iranian films made outside the state system, which tries to push past the limits that system imposes.

Underground filmmaking has become one of the few ways Iranian directors can show life as it is. Films made with a permit must follow the state's rules: women cannot appear without a headscarf, and men and women cannot touch on screen. Directors who break them risk prison and travel bans.

The film is a portrait of today's Tehran. Elaheh wants to leave Iran with her boyfriend, Soheil. She works in a secret massage parlor but refuses to offer sexual services, the "happy ending" of the title.

Mahmoudi sets out to show Elaheh's world through her relationships with her mother, her boyfriend and a society that expects different things of her. But the film's most important element is its portrait of a woman in a society on the brink of war, under pressure from every side.

On one side is a tempting offer from a "Haji," a man close to the state who invites her to his home. Elaheh badly needs the money, both to help her mother, who lives alone, pay her rent and to raise what she still needs to emigrate.

On the other side are her own instincts, her commitment to the social struggle around her and Soheil, all pointing her the other way.

The film is the story of that temptation, set in a tense society worn down by poverty.

Iran's present, and the political and social upheavals of the past year, run through it. Its ending ties the story unexpectedly to the war. There, the film steps back from its heroine and gives her a strange fate: a victim in a closed society with no way out.

Happy Ending wants to be frank and to drop every restriction of official cinema. Its characters reject compulsory hijab and have no qualms about physical contact with the opposite sex.

In that sense, it is a step forward both in getting around the censorship that governs Iranian cinema and in telling a freer story, even by the standards of underground film.

But at times it falls back on the clichés of underground cinema: drinking, drunkenness and forbidden late-night parties.

These scenes have become a staple of recent underground films that try to record the uncensored lives of Tehran's middle class. Here, though, the way they are shown and told feels repetitive, as if all these films were copying one another, and the director cannot find a different way to tell them. As a first feature, the film also has weaknesses in execution that hurt parts of it.

The film opens with a death. During protests three years earlier, Elaheh takes shelter in her father's car, and he is shot dead by security agents in front of her.

The shadow of that killing by the state hangs over the whole film. It drives Elaheh's hatred of everything to do with "them" and shapes her rebellious character.

The film struggles, however, to reach the more complex layers of its heroine and settles for watching her from a distance. That may explain the coldness of some scenes, and why the unexpected ending arrives without the audience fully feeling for her.

Listen to this article100%A shopkeeper works by lamplight inside a clothing store during a power outage in Iran.Scheduled power cuts have resumed across Iran, disrupting homes, businesses and schools, with a lawmaker saying electricity shortages could cost more than one million jobs.

People in Tehran, Isfahan, Shiraz, Mashhad, Yazd, Kermanshah and Ardebil reported hours-long outages, often without notice, in messages sent to Iran International on Sunday.

“Today, November 22, we are at school and the power has gone out. It is cloudy, and we are sitting in class in the dark,” a student in Mashhad wrote.

The disruptions have also affected water supplies and internet access.

Mohammad Allahdad, chief executive of state electricity company Tavanir, announced Saturday that residential and commercial power restrictions would begin November 22 because of fuel shortages at power plants.

Outages could last two hours every other day, increasing to two hours daily if temperatures fall further, Allahdad said.

The cuts have returned just two months after summer. During winter, increased household demand for natural gas used in heating reduces supplies available to thermal power plants, which generate most of Iran's electricity.

Economic journalist Mahtab Gholizadeh told Iran International that worsening gas shortages had disrupted electricity supplies even before severe winter weather arrived.

“Reforming energy consumption is the country's most urgent and important issue, and these reforms must begin with natural gas, not gasoline,” Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Sunday.

Natural gas accounts for 73% of Iran's energy mix, compared with 9% for gasoline, Ghalibaf added.

Electricity shortages have contributed to 600,000 job losses over the past six months by reducing industrial production, lawmaker Nasrollah Pejmanfar told parliamentary news agency Khaneh Mellat on Sunday.

More than one million workers could lose their jobs if the shortages continue, Pejmanfar added.

100%Residential buildings stand largely dark at dusk, illustrating the impact of recurring power cuts across Iran.Around 16% of electricity demand at industrial estates went unmet during the Iranian year ending March 2026, with conditions worsening since then.

Industrial operators also face charges 4.5 times official electricity tariffs, squeezing profit margins and discouraging investment, Pejmanfar said.

The outages have reached schools already struggling with inadequate heating.

Parents previously told Iran International that children attended lessons wrapped in blankets because heating systems were switched off.

“How are teachers supposed to teach and students supposed to learn with the lights off?” a Tehran resident asked, referring to President Masoud Pezeshkian's advice to conserve electricity.

Others described disruptions to water supplies and internet connections, alongside rising electricity bills.

In Arak, one person questioned why a 70-square-meter apartment had received a thirty-million-rial electricity bill despite continuing restrictions.

President Masoud Pezeshkian said November 19 that he slept wearing a jacket and extra clothing and kept his household lights switched off to save energy.

“We sold our jackets so we could put bread on the table for our wives and children for one night,” a person in Mashhad wrote to Iran International.

Others questioned whether officials' families faced similar heating shortages.

Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani raised the possibility of natural gas cuts earlier in November, while Pezeshkian said November 21 that winter shortages could create further problems.

Some Iranians attributed the recurring outages to mismanagement of the country's energy resources.

The renewed cuts have intensified pressure on households and businesses already struggling with rising costs and reduced industrial production.

Listen to this article100%A line of trucks on a road in Iran at night, as truck drivers stage strikes over rising operating costs and worsening economic conditions.Truck drivers in several Iranian cities have gone on strike over rising operating costs, stagnant freight rates and worsening economic conditions, with reports of work stoppages emerging on Sunday.

A video sent to Iran International showed a group of truck drivers stopping work in Shiraz, southern Iran, on Sunday.

The Telegram channel of the Union of Truck Drivers and Trucking Associations Across Iran also reported strikes in several cities, including Chabahar in southeastern Iran’s Sistan and Baluchestan Province and Dezful in southwestern Khuzestan Province, citing messages from its members.
